item.title: Appeal court rejects state bid to pause Bonaire climate ruling
item.description:
Appeal court rejects state bid to pause Bonaire climate ruling

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands has to draft binding national targets, the Court of Appeal in The Hague has ruled, after the state requested a suspension of its obligation.

The ruling is another step in the Bonaire climate case, which was taken to court by Greenpeace on behalf of the residents of the Dutch island in the Caribbean, where climate change is destroying the coral reef.

That case was won in January, and the court found that the government in The Hague had acted in a discriminatory manner to its people there.

Part of the ruling was that the Netherlands must set binding emissions targets for the whole economy in law by July 28, 2027, as well as draw up an adaptation plan for Bonaire that can be implemented by 2030. The ruling must be carried out even while an appeal is under way.

The government appealed the ruling in April, requesting a suspension. The Court of Appeal has largely rejected that request, but said international air and maritime transport can be left out of the targets but the government must move otherwise forward.

Marieke Vellekoop, director of Greenpeace Netherlands, said in a reaction: “The state has once again been reminded of its responsibility. Executing the judgment is not a non-binding ambition, but an obligation.”

Vellekoop said it was “incomprehensible that the state is doing everything it can to delay climate action,” while the consequences of the climate crisis are becoming increasingly severe. “On Bonaire, but also here in Europe. The cabinet must stop delaying and get to work now.”

item.title: Erasmus MC head of intensive care steps down over safety report
item.description:
Erasmus MC head of intensive care steps down over safety report

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The head of intensive care at Rotterdam’s Erasmus Medical Centre, Diederik Gommers, has stepped down in the wake of a damning report into a “culture of fear” that potentially compromised the safety of staff and patients.

The healthcare inspectorate IGJ said the situation in the department, the largest in the Netherlands, amounted to “a serious threat to the safety of patients or care”.

Gommers, who became one of the public faces of the Netherlands’ coronavirus response in 2020 when he was a member of the government’s Outbreak Management Team, quit his post with immediate effect when the findings became known this week.

The department’s board of directors has been placed under heightened supervision after the report said the psychological safety of staff was compromised by a management that did not accept being challenged or criticised.

The Erasmus MC hospital said in a statement on its website that it accepted it should have recognised the warning signs and taken action sooner.

“We are sorry that some colleagues did not feel safe enough to voice their concerns. Everyone should feel free to express their views, challenge each other and share signs.”

The hospital added that there was no suggestion patients had received substandard care as a result of the problems in the department.

18-month investigation

Inspectors began investigating the ICU 18 months ago after a whistleblower raised concerns about the workplace culture.

NOS late-night news show Nieuwsuur and regional news channel Rijnmond said they had seen hundreds of internal emails and documents going back five years and spoken to 26 current and former staff about the situation.

Doctors said “tensions” between medical specialists deterred staff from speaking out if they were critical of or worried about their colleagues’ decisions.

Jan Maarten van den Berg, a former healthcare inspector who specialised in intensive care, told Nieuwsuur: “These conclusions are very severe. There needs to be a breakthrough in the situation at Erasmus for the sake of the patients.”

Nieuwsuur earlier reported that Gommers did not have the legally required qualifications to carry out medical research on patients. The hospital said Gommers had not done any clinical research since 2023 and had started studying to obtain his certificates.

item.title: Juice and milk bottles to join deposit scheme in 2027
item.description:
Juice and milk bottles to join deposit scheme in 2027

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch packaging trade association Verpact has announced it will begin a deposit return system for plastic juice and dairy bottles on its own initiative, according to broadcaster NOS.

Plastic juice and dairy bottles of up to three litres will carry a deposit (statiegeld) from next year. Verpact said it is preparing a phased rollout in 2027. Labels, return machines, IT systems and logistics will all have to be adjusted.

The move follows pressure from climate and green growth minister Stientje van Veldhoven, who wants 90% of plastic bottles sold in the Netherlands to be collected by January 1, 2028. According to NOS, that target cannot be met without juice and dairy bottles.

In September, Van Veldhoven proposed making deposits compulsory on all plastic bottles up to three litres and banning the sale of bottles and cans without a deposit.

Dairy bottles have so far been exempt because producers say they are hard to clean, and the minister has made hygiene measures a condition. Many juice producers already charge a deposit voluntarily.

item.title: Cold comfort: Dutch skater smashes one-hour natural ice record
item.description:
Cold comfort: Dutch skater smashes one-hour natural ice record

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Marathon skater Judith Krabbenborg has taken advantage of the early cold snap to smash the world one-hour record for skating on natural ice.

The 29-year-old took to the ice in Winterswijk, Gelderland, at 8.30am on Tuesday and covered a distance of 34 kilometres 878 metres, beating the previous women’s record by 2.6 kilometres.

“I could feel my legs and my back hurting at the end, but there were so many people standing on the sidelines that it gave me energy,” she told NOS.

The previous record, set four years ago by Femke Mossinkoff, also in Winterswijk, was the first official time for the hour by a woman on natural ice. On the same day Bart Vreugdenhil set the current men’s record of 36 kilometers 717 metres.

Most skating records are set on artificial ice, but Winterswijk is one of three arenas where the local club has been able to create a natural arena for early-morning skaters during the recent cold weather.

The all-time women’s record is 40 kilometres 569 metres, set by another Dutch skater, Carien Kleibeuker, in Inzell, Austria, in 2015.

The rink at Winterswijk closed a few hours after Krabbenborg’s record-breaking skate as the ice started to melt, but it is expected to be available again on Wednesday morning.

item.title: Dutch police seek witnesses to Suriname massacre, 40 years on
item.description:
Dutch police seek witnesses to Suriname massacre, 40 years on

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch police unit for war crimes, TIM, is helping prosecutors in Suriname search for witnesses of the notorious 1986 Moiwana massacre in which at least 39 civilians were murdered by the Surinamese army.

It is believed likely that people with evidence or testimony are living in the Netherlands. The TIM put out a call for witnesses on Opsporing Verzocht, a police appeals programme, on Monday night.

The massacre occurred during Suriname’s so-called Interior War (1986-1992), a conflict between the military regime of Desi Bouterse, who seized power in a 1980 coup, and rebels led by his former bodyguard Ronnie Brunswijk. Around a third of the country’s entire population moved to the Netherlands in the years around independence in 1975.

With the massacre’s 40-year commemoration coming up, Surinamese prosecutors have asked the TIM to help revive a hunt for evidence and hold those responsible to account.

Soldiers of the army led by Desi Bouterse attacked Moiwana, which is a Maroon village close to the border with French Guiana. They were supposedly hunting Ronnie Brunswijk, a militant regime opponent who was said to be hiding in the village, though survivors say he was not there and the soldiers opened fire anyway.

The case has been stalled for decades. The police inspector leading the investigation into the incident was assassinated in 1990, and though the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled in favour of the survivors in 2005 and ordered reparations and apologies, no one has been prosecuted.

Bouterse himself became president of Suriname from 2010 to 2020. He died in 2024. Brunswijk became vice-president from 2020 to 2025. The Surinamese prosecution service reopened an inquiry in 2023 and preliminary judicial investigation began in 2025.

The 40-year commemoration will be held this coming weekend on November 29. TIM is urging anyone with information to come forward.

item.title: New HPV vaccine could save nearly 13,000 cancer diagnoses a year
item.description:
New HPV vaccine could save nearly 13,000 cancer diagnoses a year

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Nearly 13,000 people could avoid a cancer diagnosis later in life if the Netherlands raises its HPV vaccination rate, new medical research has found.

Children aged 10 are given two doses of the vaccine, which protects against a virus that causes cervical cancer in women.

A new version introduced in September covers a wider range of cancers that affect both sexes, such as vaginal and penile cancers.

Around 80% of people in the Netherlands contract the human papillomavirus, mainly though sexual activity.

Most people who are infected have no symptoms, but persistent infection is responsible for around 99.7% of all cases of cervical cancer, one of the most common types in women. Every year 1,100 women and 400 men are diagnosed with a form cancer linked to HPV, most of whom are under the age of 45.

Researchers at Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam and the Dutch cancer centre IKNL said 12,800 diagnoses could be saved if the new vaccine is given to all children who reach the age of 10 in future.

The Netherlands currently has a vaccination rate of 61% for the HPV vaccine, well below the World Health Organisation’s advisory rate of 90% for girls. Around 60% of boys have had the jab as well since the public health agency RIVM added it to their vaccine schedule in 2022.

Gynaecologist and oncologist Luc van Lonkhuijsen, of Amsterdam’s university medical centre, said many parents were anxious about side effects or dismissed it as unimportant.

“We have been vaccinating for 15 years and the number of side-effects we see is really very limited,” he told NOS.

item.title: No evidence of mental illness in suspect of Lisa’s murderer
item.description:
No evidence of mental illness in suspect of Lisa’s murderer

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Experts have found no evidence of mental disorder in the man accused of murdering Lisa from Abcoude, the 17-year-old girl whose killing last year sparked a nationwide uprising against femicide and public safety.

The public prosecution service (OM) had ordered an investigation into the mental state of the man, who calls himself Chris Jude, after he claimed he had heard voices telling him to commit rape and murder.

The findings were released in the fifth preliminary hearing of the case at Amsterdam district court on Tuesday.

He’d previously denied remembering anything about the incident, but then admitted to the crimes and said he’d been hearing voices.

On August 20 last year, Lisa phoned the police while cycling back to her parents house after a night out. She was feeling threatened by a man following her on a path through Duivendrecht.

By the time the police arrived, it was too late and her body was found. A manhunt led to Jude’s capture several days later. He was also charged with the rape and attempted rape of two other woman in Amsterdam days before murdering Lisa.

item.title: Erkens claims wolves can be culled despite EU protected status
item.description:
Erkens claims wolves can be culled despite EU protected status

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens has moved a step closer to allowing provinces to shoot wolves for population control.

Erkens said in a letter to parliament that the Netherlands could comply with EU conservation rules with 11 wolf packs, three fewer than the current number, after studying a report commissioned by his predecessor, Jean Rummenie of the farmers’ party BBB.

Experts have warned that the report by Italian independent researcher Marco Appollonio was flawed and likely to face legal challenges if he went ahead with measures based on its findings.

Rummenie ordered Appollonio to study the Dutch wolf population after rejecting an earlier analysis by Wageningen University & Research, the Netherlands’ leading agricultural college, which concluded that the Netherlands could sustainably support between 23 and 56 wolf packs.

Appolonio concluded that the wolf population in the Netherlands is “genetically healthy” and the country met the European Union’s criteria for maintaining a standing population of wolves, Erkens said.

“This confirmation that conditions in the Netherlands are favourable for a maintained population make it possible to manage wolves in the Netherlands, and that is the decision I am taking in principle,” the junior minister wrote.

Wolf-free zones

EU rules require member states to identify how many wolves they can support and recognise their place in the ecosystem as apex predators. Wolves contribute to biodiversity by controlling populations of species such as wild boar and deer and forcing them to disperse, which protects the plants they feed on.

Erkens said he wants to create wolf-free zones by asking provinces to identify areas that are suitable for wolves to roam, where they should be confined.

This would help reduce the number of confrontations with people and their pets and mean less damage caused by wolves feeding on livestock, he argued.

But ecologists say the study is likely to fall foul of EU rules because Rummenie asked Appolonio to take into account the economic impact of wolves, something the EU explicitly forbids.

The European Court of Justice said in a recent ruling against Austria that preventing loss of livestock was not a valid reason on its own for culling wolves, after a farmer was allowed to kill a wolf that had killed 20 of his sheep.

Problem wolf

Arie Trouwborst, professor of nature conservation law at Tilburg University, told NOS: “That binding report by the court has been completely ignored in the Italian report. The report from Wageningen showed that a minimum of 23 packs are needed to fulfil the [EU] criteria.”

In the Netherlands a so-called “problem wolf” was shot dead under licence last year after it attacked walkers in the near Utrecht, but only after a protracted court battle between the provincial government and conservation group Faunabescherming.

Erkens has called a national wolf summit in February where provincial and local government, vets and representatives of the tourism and recreation industry will discuss the government’s strategy.

He also plans to work more closely with Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg to draw up a common policy on wolf populations and press the EU to recognise the interests of “very small densely populated countries such as the Benelux countries.”

item.title: PTSD a growing reason for long-term sick leave among women
item.description:
PTSD a growing reason for long-term sick leave among women

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of women in their 30s applying for long-term disability benefit is expected to rise by 10% this year, with depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) the most common reasons, the AD reported on Tuesday.

Benefits agency UWV expects around 14,000 women aged 30 to 40 to apply for WIA disability benefit in 2026, the paper said. People in the Netherlands can apply for WIA after two years of sick leave, during which their employer continues to pay their wages.

Depressive episodes account for 24% of cases in this group and PTSD for 23%, followed by burn-out (7%) and overstrain (4%), according to the figures.

Debt, housing and loneliness 
“We are increasingly seeing a shift from depressive episodes and low mood to anxiety disorders such as PTSD,” UWV doctor Kevin De Decker told the paper.

De Decker said debt, housing problems, loneliness and pressure from employers were all being cited more often. Women in their 30s often have a mortgage and children, while younger women are more likely to have parents who can support them financially, he said.

Applications from men aged 30 to 40 are expected to rise by 11%, although the number of women applying is still almost twice as high. Dropout rates are highest among people working for the government, in healthcare and in education.

If you are struggling with your mental health, support is available. MIND Korrelatie offers help in Dutch and English on 0900-1450 (Monday to Friday, 9am to 9pm) or via mindkorrelatie.nl. In a crisis, contact your family doctor or call 113.

item.title: Russia lodges formal request over Destinus staff in Ukraine war
item.description:
Russia lodges formal request over Destinus staff in Ukraine war

November 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Russian embassy in The Hague says it has lodged an official request for clarification over the alleged involvement of Dutch arms company staff in military actions in the Ukraine war.

Posting on social media account X, the embassy said it had submitted the request to the Dutch ministry of foreign affairs, seeking details over “the possible involvement of the personnel of Hengelo-based company Destinus in the attacks against the Russian Federation”.

Destinus, which produces missiles and drones, publicised the use of its weapons in an attack on the Crimea bridge last week. It said it was “proud to support the Ukrainian army”.

Two days later, an investigation by the NRC found that Destinus employees had allegedly helped launch attack drones and operated interceptor drones on the battlefield.

Testimony from personnel said it had been reckless, and a drone strike in the Russian city of Voronezh injured three civilians, though it is not clear whether a Destinus drone was responsible. Destinus denies carrying out military operations and says it only provided technical support.

Experts warned that the company’s unusual public announcements could be risky, and goad Russia into targeting it with sabotage or cyber attacks.

Soon after Destinus published its involvement in the bridge strike, the Russian embassy responded asking if The Hague is “openly joining the conflict”.

The embassy has also argued that civilians who take part in hostilities lose their protected status under international law, a view the Dutch defence ministry shared with NRC.

The Dutch embassy in Kyiv was then hit during a barrage of drone strikes on the city, though it is not clear whether this was an intended target. The Netherlands summoned the Russian ambassador in response.
